newsitem.title: BELGIUM: NATO enlargement under attack on all fronts.
newsitem.headline: NATO enlargement under attack on all fronts.

text.p: NATO said on Friday it believed threats by Turkey to veto NATO enlargement over its treatment by the European Union were serious, but insisted the two issues were not linked.
"Letters must be sent to the right address, NATO cannot solve EU problems," one source said.

NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana returned from a two-day visit to Turkey on Thursday in no doubt that Ankara would carry it out its threat to block NATO enlargement at a special summit in Madrid in July.

In a succession of meetings with Turkish leaders, including President Suleyman Demirel and Islamist Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan, Solana was bluntly told the country must be taken more seriously by the European Union.
"They want progress before Madrid," said one alliance source.

Ankara, which would ultimately like full EU membership, wants to be invited to the next EU summit in Amsterdam along with some 10 former communist countries from central and eastern Europe now clamouring to join the Union.

Turkey is furious these countries appear to have moved in front of it in the queue even though the vast Moslem country is a loyal ally of the west and has been trying for years to gain closer relations with the European Union.

Last year, the EU and Turkey clinched a customs union, but key financing has not been made available to Ankara after disbursements were blocked by Greece over a host of bilateral disputes in the Aegean and eastern Mediterranean.

Dutch Foreign Minister Hans van Mierlo said on Tuesday Europe faced difficulties in fully embracing Turkey, ranging from its human rights record to its religious identity. After the comments Turkey sought reassurance on Wednesday that its Moslem identity would not block entry into the EU.
Solana's trip came at a time of renewed tension with Greece over Cyprus, which plans to buy Russian missiles to counter Turkish aircraft. Turkey has threatened to strike if they are installed.
Thursday's meeting followed an exchange of fire by Turkish and Greek Cypriots overnight in the buffer zone dividing the Mediterranean island.
